title: Mensuration: 2D Shapes and 3D Solids
why: The 2022 IPO paper asked for the distance between the tops of two poles (Pythagoras) and for the perimeter of a square built from a semicircle's diameter. Area, volume and surface-area questions are the most predictable arithmetic in the paper. The same 20 or so formulas come back every year, the numbers are chosen to cancel neatly (radius a multiple of 7, Pythagorean triplets), and each question is one or two steps once the formula is in your head.

lessons.title: Perimeter, area, volume and units
lessons.body:
### Three kinds of measurement
| Measures | Think of it as | Units |
|---|---|---|
| **Perimeter** (length) | a fence around a field | cm, m, km |
| **Area** (2D) | tiles covering a floor | cm², m², hectare |
| **Volume** (3D) | water filling a tank | cm³, m³, litre |

Quick check on any formula: perimeter uses one length, area multiplies two lengths, volume multiplies three. If your "area" formula multiplies three lengths, it is wrong.

### Unit conversions (the most common silly error)
Area is length × length, so conversion factors get **squared**. For volume they get **cubed**.

| Length | Area | Volume |
|---|---|---|
| 1 m = 100 cm | 1 m² = 10,000 cm² | 1 m³ = 10,00,000 cm³ |
| 1 km = 1000 m | 1 km² = 10,00,000 m² | 1 litre = 1000 cm³ |
| 1 cm = 10 mm | 1 hectare = 10,000 m² | 1 m³ = 1000 litres |

### Mini example
A tank holds 2.4 m³. How many litres? $2.4 \times 1000 = 2400$ litres.
A floor of 3 m² in cm²? $3 \times 10{,}000 = 30{,}000$ cm² (not 300).

### The value of π
Use $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$ when the radius is a multiple of 7 (7, 14, 21, 35 …). The answers then come out as whole numbers, which tells you the examiner intended $\frac{22}{7}$. If the options contain $\pi$, keep $\pi$ as a symbol.

### How to recognise it in the exam
Mensuration questions say "area", "perimeter", "volume", "surface area", "how many tiles/bricks/revolutions" or "litres". Before calculating, write down what is being asked (length, area or volume) and in which unit.

lessons.title: Triangles, Pythagoras and triplets
lessons.body:
### Area of a triangle
$$\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$$
The height must be **perpendicular** to the base. In a right triangle, the two shorter sides (legs) are the base and the height.

**Heron's formula** is for when you know all three sides $a, b, c$ but not the height:
$$s = \frac{a+b+c}{2}, \qquad \text{Area} = \sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$$
Here $s$ is the **semi**-perimeter (half the perimeter).

**Equilateral triangle** of side $a$: area $= \frac{\sqrt3}{4}a^2$, height $= \frac{\sqrt3}{2}a$.

### Pythagoras
In a right triangle with legs $a, b$ and hypotenuse $c$ (the longest side, opposite the right angle):
$$a^2 + b^2 = c^2$$

**Pythagorean triplets.** Memorise these. The exam uses them so that square roots come out clean:

| Triplet | Multiples you will see |
|---|---|
| 3, 4, 5 | 6-8-10, 9-12-15, 12-16-20, 15-20-25 |
| 5, 12, 13 | 10-24-26 |
| 8, 15, 17 | 16-30-34 |
| 7, 24, 25 | 14-48-50 |
| 20, 21, 29 | |
| 9, 40, 41 | |

### Mini example (IPO 2022)
Two poles of heights 13 m and 7 m stand 8 m apart. What is the distance between their tops?
- Draw it. The tops differ in height by $13 - 7 = 6$ m, and the horizontal gap is 8 m.
- These form the legs of a right triangle: distance $= \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ m (the 6-8-10 triplet).

### Heron mini example
Sides 5, 5, 6: $s = 8$; area $= \sqrt{8 \times 3 \times 3 \times 2} = \sqrt{144} = 12$.

### How to recognise it in the exam
"Ladder against a wall", "two poles", "diagonal", "distance between the tops" or "right-angled" → Pythagoras. "The sides are … find the area" with no height → Heron's formula. But first check whether it is a right triangle: for 5-12-13 you don't need Heron.

lessons.title: Quadrilaterals, paths and walls
lessons.body:
| Shape | Area | Perimeter / other |
|---|---|---|
| Square, side $a$ | $a^2$ (or $\frac{d^2}{2}$ from diagonal $d$) | $4a$; diagonal $a\sqrt2$ |
| Rectangle $l \times b$ | $lb$ | $2(l+b)$; diagonal $\sqrt{l^2+b^2}$ |
| Parallelogram | base × height | $2(a+b)$ |
| Rhombus, diagonals $d_1, d_2$ | $\frac12 d_1 d_2$ | side $= \sqrt{(\frac{d_1}{2})^2 + (\frac{d_2}{2})^2}$ |
| Trapezium, parallel sides $a, b$, height $h$ | $\frac12 (a+b) h$ | sum of the four sides |

### Why the rhombus formula works
The diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles and cut each other in half. That makes 4 right triangles with legs $\frac{d_1}{2}$ and $\frac{d_2}{2}$. So the side comes from Pythagoras, and the 4 triangles together have area $\frac12 d_1 d_2$.

### Paths and borders
For a path of width $w$ running **outside** a rectangle $l \times b$, the outer rectangle is $(l+2w) \times (b+2w)$.
$$\text{Path area} = (l+2w)(b+2w) - lb$$
The width is added on **both** sides, so it is $+2w$, not $+w$. For a path **inside** the rectangle, use $(l-2w)(b-2w)$ for the inner part.

**Four walls of a room** ($l \times b \times h$): area $= 2h(l+b)$, i.e. perimeter of the floor × height.

### Mini example
A rhombus has diagonals 24 cm and 10 cm. Area $= \frac12 \times 24 \times 10 = 120$ cm². Side $= \sqrt{12^2+5^2} = 13$ cm, so the perimeter is 52 cm.

### How to recognise it in the exam
A shape name plus "diagonal", "path", "border", "walls", "cost of fencing" or "cost of flooring". Fencing → perimeter. Tiling, flooring, painting → area.

lessons.title: Circle, semicircle, sector, ring and wheels
lessons.body:
### Circle
Radius $r$ (centre to edge), diameter $d = 2r$.

| Quantity | Formula | With $r = 7$ |
|---|---|---|
| Circumference | $2\pi r = \pi d$ | 44 |
| Area | $\pi r^2$ | 154 |

### Semicircle: the trap shape
A semicircle's boundary is **half the curve plus the straight diameter**:
$$\text{Perimeter} = \pi r + 2r = r(\pi + 2) = \frac{36}{7} r$$
Area $= \frac12 \pi r^2$.

### Sector (a "pizza slice") with angle $\theta$ degrees
$$\text{Arc length} = \frac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r, \qquad \text{Area} = \frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$$
Perimeter of the sector = arc + $2r$. A quadrant is a sector with $\theta = 90^\circ$.

### Ring (annulus) between radii $R$ and $r$
Area $= \pi(R^2 - r^2) = \pi(R+r)(R-r)$.

### Wheels
One revolution of a wheel covers one circumference. Number of revolutions $= \dfrac{\text{distance}}{2\pi r}$, with both in the same unit.

### Mini example
A semicircle of radius 7 cm: perimeter $= \frac{22}{7} \times 7 + 14 = 22 + 14 = 36$ cm; area $= \frac12 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 49 = 77$ cm².

A wheel of radius 21 cm has circumference $2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 21 = 132$ cm, so in 1.32 km $= 1{,}32{,}000$ cm it turns $132000 / 132 = 1000$ times.

### How to recognise it in the exam
"Circular", "wheel", "revolutions", "semicircular", "quadrant", "ring" or "track". If the radius is a multiple of 7, use $\frac{22}{7}$. If the question says "perimeter of a semicircle", include the diameter.

lessons.title: Cube, cuboid and cylinder
lessons.body:
### Surface area vs volume
- **Volume** = the space inside (how much water it holds), in unit³.
- **Total surface area (TSA)** = area of all faces (paint for the whole box), in unit².
- **Lateral / curved surface area (LSA/CSA)** = only the sides, without top and bottom (the label on a can, the four walls of a room).

| Solid | Volume | Lateral / curved SA | Total SA | Longest diagonal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cuboid $l, b, h$ | $lbh$ | $2h(l+b)$ | $2(lb+bh+hl)$ | $\sqrt{l^2+b^2+h^2}$ |
| Cube, side $a$ | $a^3$ | $4a^2$ | $6a^2$ | $a\sqrt3$ |
| Cylinder $r, h$ | $\pi r^2 h$ | $2\pi r h$ | $2\pi r(r+h)$ | — |

### Why the cylinder formulas look like that
Volume = (area of the circular base) × height $= \pi r^2 \times h$. Unroll the curved surface and it becomes a rectangle of width $2\pi r$ (the circumference) and height $h$, so CSA $= 2\pi r h$. Add the two circular lids, $2\pi r^2$, to get the total.

### Mini example
Cylinder with $r = 7$ cm, $h = 10$ cm:
- Volume $= \frac{22}{7} \times 49 \times 10 = 1540$ cm³
- CSA $= 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 10 = 440$ cm²
- TSA $= 440 + 2 \times 154 = 748$ cm²

### How to recognise it in the exam
"Box", "room", "tank", "pipe", "roller", "can" or "pillar". Painting walls → lateral area; painting the whole box → TSA; filling → volume. For a roller, the area covered in one revolution = its CSA.

lessons.title: Cone, sphere, hemisphere and frustum
lessons.body:
### Cone
A cone has radius $r$, vertical height $h$ and **slant height** $l$ (measured along the sloping side). These three form a right triangle:
$$l = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$$

| Solid | Volume | Curved SA | Total SA |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cone | $\frac13 \pi r^2 h$ | $\pi r l$ | $\pi r(l + r)$ |
| Sphere | $\frac43 \pi r^3$ | $4\pi r^2$ (the whole surface) | $4\pi r^2$ |
| Hemisphere | $\frac23 \pi r^3$ | $2\pi r^2$ | $3\pi r^2$ (curved + flat circle) |
| Frustum (cone with top cut off), radii $R, r$, height $h$ | $\frac13 \pi h (R^2 + r^2 + Rr)$ | $\pi (R + r) l$, where $l = \sqrt{h^2 + (R-r)^2}$ | CSA $+ \pi R^2 + \pi r^2$ |

### Memory links
- A cone holds $\frac13$ of a cylinder with the same base and height.
- Volume uses the **height $h$**; curved surface uses the **slant height $l$**. Mixing these up is the #1 cone mistake.
- Hemisphere TSA $3\pi r^2$ = curved $2\pi r^2$ + flat lid $\pi r^2$.
- A frustum is a bucket or a lampshade.

### Mini example
Cone with $r = 5$, $h = 12$: $l = \sqrt{25 + 144} = 13$ (5-12-13 triplet).
- CSA $= \pi \times 5 \times 13 = 65\pi$
- TSA $= \pi \times 5 \times (13 + 5) = 90\pi$
- Volume $= \frac13 \pi \times 25 \times 12 = 100\pi$

### How to recognise it in the exam
"Conical tent" (canvas needed = CSA), "ice-cream cone", "ball", "bowl" (hemisphere), "bucket" (frustum). Tents ask for canvas → curved surface. Heaps of grain ask for volume.

lessons.title: Melting, recasting and percentage change
lessons.body:
### Melting and recasting
When a solid is melted and reshaped, the **volume stays the same** (surface area does not).
$$\text{Volume of original} = \text{Volume of new solid(s)}$$
Number of small pieces $= \dfrac{\text{volume of big solid}}{\text{volume of one small piece}}$.

Cancel $\pi$ and common factors **before** multiplying and the arithmetic becomes tiny.

### Mini example
A sphere of radius 3 cm is melted and recast into a cylinder of radius 2 cm. Find the height.
$$\frac43 \pi (3^3) = \pi (2^2) h \Rightarrow 36 = 4h \Rightarrow h = 9 \text{ cm}$$

### Water level rising
Drop a solid into a tank of water: volume of the solid = base area of the tank × rise in water level.

### Scaling: what happens when dimensions change
If every length is multiplied by $k$:
- perimeter × $k$
- area × $k^2$
- volume × $k^3$

| Change in every side | Area change | Volume change |
|---|---|---|
| +10% ($k=1.1$) | +21% | +33.1% |
| +20% ($k=1.2$) | +44% | +72.8% |
| +50% ($k=1.5$) | +125% | +237.5% |
| doubled ($k=2$) | ×4 (+300%) | ×8 (+700%) |

Shortcut for area when the two sides change by $x\%$ and $y\%$: net change $= x + y + \frac{xy}{100}$ %.

### How to recognise it in the exam
"Melted", "recast", "how many balls/coins/bricks can be made", "water level rises" or "each side is increased by …%".

formulas.name: Square and rectangle
formulas.tex: A_{sq} = a^2 = \frac{d^2}{2},\ d = a\sqrt2;\quad A_{rect} = lb,\ P = 2(l+b),\ d = \sqrt{l^2+b^2}

formulas.name: Path of width w outside a rectangle
Circle and ring
formulas.tex: C = 2\pi r,\quad A = \pi r^2,\quad A_{ring} = \pi (R^2 - r^2)

formulas.name: Cube
formulas.tex: V = a^3,\quad TSA = 6a^2,\quad LSA = 4a^2,\quad d = a\sqrt3

formulas.name: Cylinder
formulas.tex: V = \pi r^2 h,\quad CSA = 2\pi r h,\quad TSA = 2\pi r(r+h)

formulas.name: Cone
formulas.tex: l = \sqrt{r^2+h^2},\quad V = \frac13 \pi r^2 h,\quad CSA = \pi r l,\quad TSA = \pi r(l+r)

examples.q: Find the area of a triangle whose sides are 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm.
examples.solution:
Step 1: $s = \frac{13 + 14 + 15}{2} = 21$.
Step 2: $s - a = 8$, $s - b = 7$, $s - c = 6$.
Step 3: Area $= \sqrt{21 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6} = \sqrt{7056} = 84$ cm².
Answer: 84 cm²
examples.shortcut: 13-14-15 is two right triangles glued together: 5-12-13 and 9-12-15 share the height 12 on the base 14. Area $= \frac12 \times 14 \times 12 = 84$.

examples.q:
Two vertical poles 18 m and 9 m high stand 12 m apart on level ground. Find the distance between their tops.
(a) 15 m (b) 21 m (c) 12 m (d) 27 m
examples.solution:
Step 1: Difference in heights $= 18 - 9 = 9$ m (vertical leg).
Step 2: Horizontal gap $= 12$ m (horizontal leg).
Step 3: Distance $= \sqrt{9^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{81 + 144} = \sqrt{225} = 15$ m.
Answer: (a) 15 m
examples.shortcut: 9-12-15 is 3 × (3-4-5). Use the DIFFERENCE of heights, never the sum.

examples.q:
(IPO 2022) The perimeter of a semicircle is 180 cm. The side of a square is 60% more than the diameter of the semicircle. Find the perimeter of the square.
(a) 448 cm (b) 280 cm (c) 360 cm (d) 112 cm
examples.solution:
Step 1: Perimeter of a semicircle $= \pi r + 2r = \frac{36}{7} r$.
Step 2: $\frac{36}{7} r = 180 \Rightarrow r = 180 \times \frac{7}{36} = 35$ cm. Diameter $= 70$ cm.
Step 3: Side of square $= 70 + 60\% \text{ of } 70 = 70 \times 1.6 = 112$ cm.
Step 4: Perimeter $= 4 \times 112 = 448$ cm.
Answer: (a) 448 cm
examples.shortcut: Remember $\pi + 2 = \frac{36}{7}$ with $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$. Option (d) is the side, not the perimeter.

examples.q: A wheel of radius 35 cm rolls along a road. How many revolutions does it make in covering 1.1 km?
examples.solution:
Step 1: Circumference $= 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 35 = 220$ cm.
Step 2: Distance $= 1.1$ km $= 1{,}10{,}000$ cm.
Step 3: Revolutions $= 110000 / 220 = 500$.
Answer: 500

examples.q: A room is 8 m long, 6 m wide and 4 m high. Find the cost of painting its four walls at ₹20 per m².
examples.solution:
Step 1: Area of four walls $= 2h(l + b) = 2 \times 4 \times (8 + 6) = 112$ m².
Step 2: Cost $= 112 \times 20 = $ ₹2240.
Answer: ₹2240
examples.shortcut: Four walls = perimeter of the floor × height $= 28 \times 4$.

examples.q: A conical tent has base radius 7 m and height 24 m. Find (a) the canvas needed and (b) the volume of air inside.
examples.solution:
Step 1: Slant height $l = \sqrt{7^2 + 24^2} = \sqrt{625} = 25$ m.
Step 2: Canvas = curved surface $= \pi r l = \frac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 25 = 550$ m².
Step 3: Volume $= \frac13 \pi r^2 h = \frac13 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 49 \times 24 = 1232$ m³.
Answer: 550 m²; 1232 m³
examples.shortcut: 7-24-25 triplet gives $l$ instantly. Canvas uses $l$, volume uses $h$.

examples.q: A hemispherical bowl of internal radius 9 cm is full of liquid. The liquid is poured into cylindrical bottles of radius 1.5 cm and height 4 cm. How many bottles are needed?
examples.solution:
Step 1: Volume of bowl $= \frac23 \pi r^3 = \frac23 \pi \times 729 = 486\pi$.
Step 2: Volume of one bottle $= \pi \times 1.5^2 \times 4 = 9\pi$.
Step 3: Number of bottles $= \frac{486\pi}{9\pi} = 54$.
Answer: 54
examples.shortcut: Never substitute $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$ when it cancels anyway.

examples.q: Each edge of a cube is increased by 50%. Find the percentage increase in (a) its surface area and (b) its volume.
examples.solution:
Step 1: New edge $= 1.5a$, so the scale factor is $k = 1.5$.
Step 2: Surface area × $k^2 = 2.25$ → increase of 125%.
Step 3: Volume × $k^3 = 3.375$ → increase of 237.5%.
Answer: 125%; 237.5%

traps: Unit squaring: 1 m² = 10,000 cm² (not 100) and 1 m³ = 10,00,000 cm³. Convert lengths first, then calculate.
Perimeter of a semicircle is πr + 2r. Leaving out the diameter (2r) gives only the curved part.
Radius vs diameter: if the question gives a diameter, halve it before using πr² or 2πr.
Cone: curved surface uses the slant height l = √(r² + h²); volume uses the vertical height h.
Hemisphere: curved SA = 2πr², total SA = 3πr². Read whether the question says 'curved' or 'total'.
Heron's formula needs s = HALF the perimeter. Using the full perimeter makes every bracket wrong.
Two poles: use the DIFFERENCE of heights as one leg, not the sum.
Percentage change: if every side goes up 20%, area goes up 44% and volume 72.8%, not 20%.

practice.q: The area of a triangle with sides 5 cm, 12 cm and 13 cm is:
practice.explanation:
$5^2 + 12^2 = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13^2$, so it is a right triangle with legs 5 and 12.
Area $= \frac12 \times 5 \times 12 = 30$ cm².
Answer: (b) 30 cm²

practice.q: The area of a square whose diagonal is 12 cm is:
practice.explanation:
Area of a square from its diagonal $= \frac{d^2}{2}$.
$= \frac{144}{2} = 72$ cm².
(144 would be correct only if 12 were the side.)
Answer: (a) 72 cm²

practice.q: The circumference of a circle of radius 14 cm is (take $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$):
practice.explanation:
Circumference $= 2\pi r = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 14$.
$= 2 \times 22 \times 2 = 88$ cm.
(616 is the area; 44 is only $\pi r$.)
Answer: (c) 88 cm

practice.q: The volume of a cube of edge 5 cm is:
practice.explanation:
Volume $= a^3 = 5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125$ cm³.
(150 is the total surface area $6a^2$.)
Answer: (d) 125 cm³

practice.q: 2.5 hectares is equal to:
The diagonals of a rhombus are 16 cm and 12 cm. Its area is:
practice.explanation:
Area of a rhombus $= \frac12 d_1 d_2$.
$= \frac12 \times 16 \times 12 = 96$ cm².
(192 forgets the $\frac12$; 40 cm is the perimeter.)
Answer: (a) 96 cm²

practice.q: The volume of a cylinder of radius 3.5 cm and height 20 cm is (take $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$):
practice.explanation:
$V = \pi r^2 h = \frac{22}{7} \times 3.5 \times 3.5 \times 20$.
$= 22 \times 0.5 \times 3.5 \times 20 = 770$ cm³.
(440 is the curved surface area $2\pi r h$; 3080 uses 7 as the radius.)
Answer: (b) 770 cm³

practice.q: The surface area of a sphere of radius 7 cm is (take $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$):
practice.explanation:
Surface area $= 4\pi r^2 = 4 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 49$.
$= 4 \times 154 = 616$ cm².
(1437.33 is the volume; 308 is a hemisphere's curved surface.)
Answer: (d) 616 cm²

practice.q: Two vertical poles 11 m and 6 m high stand 12 m apart. The distance between their tops is:
practice.explanation:
Difference in heights $= 11 - 6 = 5$ m; horizontal gap $= 12$ m.
Distance $= \sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13$ m.
(20.8 m comes from wrongly using the sum 17 as a leg.)
Answer: (d) 13 m
Shortcut: 5-12-13 triplet.

practice.q: The area of a triangle with sides 26 cm, 28 cm and 30 cm is:
practice.explanation:
$s = \frac{26 + 28 + 30}{2} = 42$.
$s - a = 16$, $s - b = 14$, $s - c = 12$.
Area $= \sqrt{42 \times 16 \times 14 \times 12} = \sqrt{112896} = 336$ cm².
Answer: (a) 336 cm²
Shortcut: 26-28-30 is 2 × (13-14-15), whose area is 84; area scales by $2^2$: $4 \times 84 = 336$.

practice.q: The perimeter of a semicircular plate of radius 21 cm is (take $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$):
practice.explanation:
Perimeter of a semicircle $= \pi r + 2r$.
$= \frac{22}{7} \times 21 + 42 = 66 + 42 = 108$ cm.
(66 forgets the diameter; 132 is the full circle.)
Answer: (c) 108 cm
Shortcut: $\frac{36}{7} \times 21 = 108$.

practice.q: A wheel has a diameter of 70 cm. How many revolutions will it make to cover 1.76 km?
practice.explanation:
Circumference $= \pi d = \frac{22}{7} \times 70 = 220$ cm.
Distance $= 1.76$ km $= 1{,}76{,}000$ cm.
Revolutions $= \frac{176000}{220} = 800$.
(400 comes from treating 70 as the radius.)
Answer: (b) 800

practice.q: The curved surface area of a cone of base radius 6 cm and height 8 cm is:
practice.explanation:
Slant height $l = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = 10$ cm.
CSA $= \pi r l = \pi \times 6 \times 10 = 60\pi$ cm².
($48\pi$ wrongly uses the height 8; $96\pi$ is the total surface area.)
Answer: (d) $60\pi$ cm²

practice.q: The total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius 7 cm is (take $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$):
practice.explanation:
TSA of a solid hemisphere = curved $2\pi r^2$ + flat circle $\pi r^2 = 3\pi r^2$.
$= 3 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 49 = 3 \times 154 = 462$ cm².
(308 is only the curved part; 718.67 is the volume.)
Answer: (b) 462 cm²

practice.q: The perimeter of a semicircle is 72 cm. The side of a square is 25% more than the diameter of the semicircle. The perimeter of the square is (take $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$):
practice.explanation:
$\pi r + 2r = \frac{36}{7} r = 72 \Rightarrow r = 14$ cm, so diameter $= 28$ cm.
Side $= 28 \times 1.25 = 35$ cm.
Perimeter $= 4 \times 35 = 140$ cm.
(112 forgets the 25% increase; 229.1 forgets the diameter in the semicircle's perimeter.)
Answer: (a) 140 cm

practice.q: A room is 6 m long, 4 m wide and 3 m high. The area of its four walls is:
practice.explanation:
Area of four walls $= 2h(l + b)$.
$= 2 \times 3 \times (6 + 4) = 60$ m².
(72 is the volume in m³; 108 is the total surface area; 84 adds the floor.)
Answer: (c) 60 m²

practice.q: The area of a sector of a circle of radius 21 cm with central angle $60^\circ$ is (take $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$):
practice.explanation:
Area $= \frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2 = \frac{60}{360} \times \frac{22}{7} \times 441$.
$= \frac16 \times 1386 = 231$ cm².
(22 is the arc length in cm.)
Answer: (b) 231 cm²

practice.q: The length of the longest rod that can be placed in a box of dimensions 12 cm × 4 cm × 3 cm is:
practice.explanation:
Longest rod = diagonal of the cuboid $= \sqrt{l^2 + b^2 + h^2}$.
$= \sqrt{144 + 16 + 9} = \sqrt{169} = 13$ cm.
(19 adds the sides; 169 forgets the square root.)
Answer: (d) 13 cm

practice.q: A solid metal sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and recast into a solid cylinder of radius 4 cm. The height of the cylinder is:
practice.explanation:
Volume is unchanged: $\frac43 \pi r^3 = \pi R^2 h$.
$\frac43 \times 216 = 16h$.
$288 = 16h \Rightarrow h = 18$ cm.
(9 cm uses the hemisphere formula $\frac23 \pi r^3$.)
Answer: (c) 18 cm

practice.q: A solid cone of base radius 6 cm and height 24 cm is melted and recast into small spheres of radius 2 cm each. The number of spheres formed is:
practice.explanation:
Volume of cone $= \frac13 \pi \times 36 \times 24 = 288\pi$.
Volume of one sphere $= \frac43 \pi \times 8 = \frac{32}{3}\pi$.
Number $= 288\pi \div \frac{32\pi}{3} = \frac{288 \times 3}{32} = 27$.
(81 forgets the $\frac13$ in the cone's volume.)
Answer: (a) 27

practice.q: Each edge of a cube is decreased by 10%. The percentage decrease in its volume is:
practice.explanation:
New edge $= 0.9a$.
New volume $= (0.9)^3 a^3 = 0.729 a^3$.
Decrease $= 1 - 0.729 = 0.271$, i.e. $27.1\%$.
(19% is the decrease in surface area, $1 - 0.81$; 30% simply triples 10%.)
Answer: (b) 27.1%

practice.q: A bucket is in the form of a frustum of a cone with radii of its ends 20 cm and 8 cm and depth 16 cm. Its curved surface area is:
practice.explanation:
Slant height $l = \sqrt{h^2 + (R - r)^2} = \sqrt{16^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{400} = 20$ cm.
CSA $= \pi (R + r) l = \pi \times 28 \times 20 = 560\pi$ cm².
($448\pi$ wrongly uses the depth 16; $1024\pi$ adds both circular ends.)
Answer: (d) $560\pi$ cm²
Shortcut: 12-16-20 is 4 × (3-4-5).

practice.q: The hypotenuse of a right triangle is 26 cm and its area is 120 cm². Its perimeter is:
practice.explanation:
Let the legs be $a, b$: $\frac12 ab = 120 \Rightarrow ab = 240$, and $a^2 + b^2 = 676$.
$(a + b)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + 2ab = 676 + 480 = 1156 \Rightarrow a + b = 34$.
Perimeter $= 34 + 26 = 60$ cm. (The legs are 10 and 24.)
(34 forgets to add the hypotenuse.)
Answer: (b) 60 cm
Shortcut: 10-24-26 is 2 × (5-12-13); check $\frac12 \times 10 \times 24 = 120$ ✓.

practice.q: A square is inscribed in a circle of radius 7 cm. The area of the square is:
practice.explanation:
The diagonal of the square = diameter of the circle $= 14$ cm.
Area of square $= \frac{d^2}{2} = \frac{196}{2} = 98$ cm².
(196 treats 14 as the side; 154 is the circle's area.)
Answer: (c) 98 cm²

practice.q: A rectangular garden 40 m × 30 m has a path 2.5 m wide running all around it on the outside. The area of the path is:
practice.explanation:
Outer rectangle $= (40 + 5) \times (30 + 5) = 45 \times 35 = 1575$ m².
Garden $= 40 \times 30 = 1200$ m².
Path $= 1575 - 1200 = 375$ m².
(350 = perimeter × width, which misses the 4 corner squares; 181.25 adds the width only once.)
Answer: (a) 375 m²
Shortcut: $2w(l + b) + 4w^2 = 350 + 25 = 375$.
